top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits a specific, mature scientific contribution: transparent, re-run research designs showing that import competition and technological change produce large, persistent local labour-market adjustment costs and job polarisation. The core finding has survived more than a decade of replication and challenge, and the debate is over magnitudes and shift-share inference, not whether the costs exist. Attribution is tightest on the empirical evidence. Dorn co-authored the China-shock papers and Autor and Dorn (2013) spans polarisation, so the citation can stay empirical and avoid claiming the task theory of Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo. The Katz variant (P002) is close and defensible, since it credits the older wage-structure evidence. I rank it second because Katz's education-and-technology work sits near the Goldin research recognised in 2023, which makes his marginal credit harder to delineate, and because a broad citation invites the charge of bundling two discoveries. P003 (Melitz, Helpman) has a compact core but unresolved priority claims (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and a contested size of welfare gains. P004 (BLP) is a mature and credible methods contribution with narrower reach and an open Bresnahan attribution question. Every proposal with an identifiable discovery ranks above no award.
recusal_note: No personal tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Melitz, Helpman, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn is apparent from the profile; my frequent co-authors are credited on no proposal. For transparency, I presented the 2023 prize to Goldin, and Katz is a long-time Goldin co-author, which bears on the marginal-credit judgement for P002. My field (labour economics) is adjacent to B009. Disclosed and not adjudicated; no independent verification claimed.
